title: Loss of the big bands and the missing farm system
summary: Jones argues that after the war the dance floors and big bands vanished, leaving young players with no way to come up.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: He was a kid, you know, along with Michael and what have you. I said, "Why don't you just learn how to touch the drums, like your father?" But you must remember, Milt, that the experience coming out of the World War II, they took the dance floor away. They took the big bands away. Now the best the kid could do was sit and play at a corner bar somewhere and take some four bars and play within that framework. The consistency was broken. We've had a consistency broken for the last 22 years and we've had so much wealth of talent out here. You know that, with the young bass players you hang out with, the young guitarists, the young pianists. But where are they going to get a chance to matriculate, you see. It's too bad in the music business we don't have like they do in baseball or basketball where they have the farm systems.
Berry used to always say they should have major and minor league in music like there is in baseball.

We had that. When you was in this category you played into this club. You did not go over here and play into this club until you qualified, then you begin to move up and you sit in over here. Then as I said, the older guys when they got ready to semi-retire, they went and got a young man and set him down in the home and gave him the book and they went to the bandleader and said, "He's taking my place."
